summary: The past 30 sessions show a burst-clustering pattern: multiple short sessions open in rapid succession on the same day (e.g. 5 sessions within 2 hours on 2026-05-14), suggesting iterative debugging or feature-spike work rather than single sustained sessions. Session cadence is uneven — heavy days cluster around May 8, 11–12, and 14–16, with gaps in between, pointing to project-sprint rhythms rather than daily steady work. No clear evidence of abandoned sessions from metadata alone, though the high density of same-day multi-session starts may indicate sessions that ended early and were restarted.

insights.name: same-day session burst clustering
insights.instruction: Watch for sessions that open within 10–30 minutes of a prior session close on the same project — these are likely context-loss restarts. Cross-reference with /core-dump and /catchup usage to see if checkpoint discipline is holding.

insights.name: sprint-gap-sprint cadence across project days
insights.instruction: Session density spikes on ~3-4 active days per week with 1-2 day gaps. If a project memory or checkpoint was written before the gap, verify it's being loaded at the start of the next sprint day via /catchup.

insights.name: mid-day session concentration
insights.instruction: Most sessions start between 11:00–16:00 UTC. If sessions consistently end before context is serialized (no /core-dump), runtime-notes and WAL entries from these sessions may be incomplete. Watch for sessions that span less than 30 minutes — those are the highest-risk for orphaned context.

The burst-restart pattern correlates with the user's known heavy /catchup and /core-dump reliance (see feedback_session_continuity.md). Bursts that don't use /catchup at session open are the gap to close.

summary: The 170-session delta (June 12–July 11, 2026) is dominated by near-simultaneous session pair launches — multiple instances where two sessions start within seconds to a few minutes of each other — consistent with heavy multi-agent fan-out use. Session starts cluster in the 07:00–11:30 UTC window, matching an IST afternoon primary work cadence, with a secondary evening sprint cluster at 18:00–21:00 UTC. Orphaned and short-lived sessions remain frequent across the full period, signaling a high rate of abrupt task hand-offs or context resets.

insights.name: concurrent-session-pair-spawning
insights.instruction: Watch for paired session IDs within ±5 min in future deltas; if both sessions in a pair touch the same project, surface it — two agents on the same codebase simultaneously is the contain-subagent-token-sprawl risk pattern.

insights.name: utc-morning-session-clustering
insights.instruction: Use as anomaly baseline: sessions outside 05:00–14:00 UTC that are also multi-turn or error-heavy may indicate crisis/deadline pressure — worth correlating with atone error-rate spikes in the same date range.

insights.name: late-utc-evening-sprint-cluster
insights.instruction: If late-UTC sessions cluster around project deadline dates visible in memory, flag in the weekly summary — same-day AM+PM double sessions could indicate a crunch cycle worth surfacing.

insights.name: high-orphan-session-rate
insights.instruction: Cross-reference with atone `declared-ready-without-runtime-exercise` (9x, still recurring): orphaned sessions whose last recorded tool was a Bash command with no subsequent read/verify call are the highest-risk subset — they may represent the exact failure mode the hook is trying to catch, mid-session.

summary: The 27-session window spans July 9–13 and shows two distinct session shapes: a tight parallel fan-out burst on July 11 (six sessions launched within ~2 minutes) and a high-density interactive day on July 13 (12 sessions across 16 hours). Inter-day coverage is sparse — four days total, with July 9 and July 12 each contributing a single session — suggesting work is concentrated in short intense bursts rather than distributed across the week. No July 14 sessions appear, possibly indicating a natural wind-down after the July 13 peak.

insights.name: parallel-agent-fanout-burst
insights.instruction: Watch for recurrence: if a future fan-out burst also produces orphan WAL entries or unread mail (5 such dead sessions already flagged in the session-start reminder), the fan-out may be systematically failing to clean up child agents. Cross-reference with atone `unprompted-infra-scope-creep` if the fan-out was self-initiated.

insights.name: single-day-session-concentration
insights.instruction: High session counts on a single day often indicate task fragmentation — user clearing context repeatedly rather than using /compact. Watch for a matching spike in orphan checkpoints or WAL entries on July 13. If confirmed, this is a candidate for a memory note on the user's compaction habits.

insights.name: early-morning-july13-interactive-burst
insights.instruction: Without message counts this remains tentative. If the sessions tool surfaces low assistant-message counts here relative to user messages, escalate to a stuck-task pattern — short sequential sessions on the same morning can signal the user hitting a blocker and retrying.

insights.name: sparse-interday-coverage
insights.instruction: Track whether this burst-and-gap cadence persists across future windows. If it does, it is a stable user work-rhythm signal worth saving to memory (user works in multi-session sprint days with off-days between). If July 14+ shows a return to activity, this was a normal weekend gap rather than a structural pattern.

summary: Eighteen sessions over six days show a pronounced spike on 2026-07-14 (11 of 18 sessions, 61%) with repeated evidence of parallel session pairs starting within seconds of each other, pointing to multi-agent orchestration rather than sequential single-user work. Session-close health is degraded: three orphan turn-state files from recent sessions indicate abrupt termination rather than clean close, likely correlated with the high parallel volume. The tmp project dominates session space, consistent with the 76% drift rate already captured in analytics.

insights.name: parallel-session-bursts
insights.instruction: Watch for IPC coordination gaps: pairs sess-a0f35401/sess-6b120b0a (9s apart) and sess-37d08f61/sess-7c520f34 (43s apart) and sess-8b93756c/sess-5f3a4812 (53s apart) each launched faster than a human could start them sequentially. Flag future same-day session pairs with <60s gap as orchestrated multi-agent work; confirm they pre-negotiated task ownership via IPC before starting edits (see lessons[0.83] in dream digest).

insights.name: july-14-density-spike
insights.instruction: 11 of 18 sessions on a single calendar day spanning 08:37–21:24 UTC suggests an intensive orchestration run or planned sprint. If a similar single-day spike recurs, check whether orphan counts also rise that day — the July-14 burst precedes the three orphan files noted for July-15, suggesting the density itself stresses clean-close discipline.

insights.name: session-orphan-correlation
insights.instruction: Three orphan turn-state files logged for July-15 follow the July-14 density spike. Hypothesis: high parallel session counts leave some sessions without a supervising parent to send the stop signal, producing abrupt termination. Watch whether orphan count correlates with parallel-burst days in future passes; if confirmed, surface as a graduation candidate for a rule requiring parent TaskStop on verified sub-agents.

insights.name: tmp-project-dominance
insights.instruction: Session analytics already record 76% drift rate; this cohort reinforces it. Most sessions resolve to /private/tmp rather than a named project root, which means session-scoped checkpoints and WAL files accumulate in a transient directory. Flag if any session in tmp appears to carry load-bearing output (research synthesis, design docs) without an explicit write to a durable path before close.
